title: Vocabulary term
description:
ONE canonical term of a governed vocabulary — `high-throughput` of `network_tier`, `gold` of `storage_tier` — carried by a record keyed to (`vocabulary_kind`, `scope`).

WHERE THIS CAME FROM. A term used to be a `layer` with `layer_type: reference_data`, and that was two things wearing one hat. ADR-054 retired the layer form because context is never merged into an assembly, so it was never a layer; ADR-058 settles where the terms go instead — and its answer is this record, keyed rather than layered (ADR-058 Q1: keyed records keep a large vocabulary out of the Class artifact and preserve independent curation).

WHAT THE MOVE BUYS, which is the whole reason it is not a rename. A reference-data layer sat OUTSIDE both enforcements the model already had. This record sits inside both:

  - `scope` puts the term at a Class position, and the scope position IS the portability contract (ADR-038 §3). A term canonical at `Network` is portable to every Network provider; one at a Provider scope is that provider's. Before, a vocabulary had no scope at all, which is exactly why `os_image` and `vm_size` came to "mean many things" — nothing said WHERE a meaning held.
  - `curation_state` puts it on the vocabulary-intake ladder (ADR-039), so `proposed → canonical` is a state the record carries rather than a convention around it.

THE TERM DENOTES A FLOOR, NOT A LABEL (ADR-036). `requirements` carries what the name actually promises — `high-throughput` means at least 10G-class and sub-millisecond, and any provider clearing that qualifies. The match is against the floor, never the string, which is the only reason a term survives leaving the estate that coined it. A term with no floor is a label, and two estates' labels are incomparable by construction.

NOT A TAXONOMY TERM, and the distinction is load-bearing. `Knowledge.TaxonomyTerm` carries a CATEGORY — what a thing IS (`dmz`, `management`), with normalization rules so five spellings converge. This carries a FLOOR — what a thing must MEET. `network_zone` is a taxonomy because a zone is a classification; `network_tier` is a vocabulary term because a tier is a measurable minimum. Collapsing them would put normalization rules on a floor and minima on a category.

uuid.description: Frozen identity (ADR-051). A content change bumps `version`; the uuid never moves.

handle.description: The authoring name. A reference is AUTHORED by handle and RESOLVED to the uuid form (WIR-004) — never resolved by name alone.

version.description: A published (identity, version) is immutable: change the floor, bump the version. A consumer pinned to a version is pinned to the promise that version made.

vocabulary_kind.description: The vocabulary this term belongs to — `network_tier`, `storage_tier`, `os_image`, `vm_size`. Half the key. A `SharedDataElement` names this kind in `values.reference_data_type` to declare that its values are governed rather than an inline enum (ADR-038 §2).

scope.description:
The Class scope this term is canonical AT — the other half of the key, and the portability contract (ADR-038 §3, ADR-058 §2).

Read it as the answer to "how far does this meaning travel?" A term at `Network` holds for every Network provider; the same name at `Network.Fabric.AcmeSDN` holds only there. Portable reliance on a term requires it be canonical at a scope at least as general as the consumer's — which is checkable in a diff rather than asserted in prose, and promoted by the governed contribution operation rather than by editing a copy.

term.description: The selectable name — what a consumer writes. Portable because of what `requirements` says it means, not because the string matches.

curation_state.description: Where this term sits on the intake ladder. Whether an estate may BIND a term that is not yet `canonical` is a profile floor (ADR-007), not a property of the term.

requirements.description:
The FLOOR the term denotes — what a provider must clear to qualify (ADR-036). Kind-specific by nature: a `network_tier` states bandwidth and latency minima, a `storage_tier` states IOPS and throughput. Open by construction because UDLM does not know every vocabulary an estate will govern; what it does know is that a term with no floor cannot be compared across estates, which is why at least one property is required.

This is the data that used to sit in a layer's `fields`. It never was a contribution to an assembled payload — nothing merged it — which is the plainest evidence the layer form was wrong.

status.description: Lifecycle, distinct from `curation_state`. A term can be `canonical` and `deprecated` at once: canonical says the ladder promoted it, deprecated says stop using it. Collapsing the two would make "retire a term" indistinguishable from "the ladder rejected it".

contributor.description: Who may author this term and the review it requires (federated-contribution-model §3).

supersedes.description: The term record(s) this one replaces, by uuid — never edit a published term, supersede it (ADR-051).

examples.name: Network tier — high throughput
examples.description: Governed definition of the 'high-throughput' network tier.

requirements.description: 10G-class or better with sub-millisecond intra-segment latency.
